title: Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
intro: This guide explains what Ontario's Human Rights Code says about equal treatment and harassment, how an application to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario works, what the Tribunal can order, and when a court can deal with a human rights claim. It describes the law generally and does not say how it applies to anyone's situation.

sections.heading: Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment
paragraphs: Part I of the Code is headed Freedom from Discrimination. It gives every person a right to equal treatment “with respect to services, goods and facilities” and “with respect to the occupancy of accommodation”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 1, 2 (1))

Part I also covers contracts, employment and vocational associations. Every person having legal capacity “has a right to contract on equal terms”. Every person has a right to equal treatment “with respect to employment”, and with respect to “membership in any trade union, trade or occupational association or self-governing profession”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 3, 5 (1), 6)

The Code also says: “No person shall infringe or do, directly or indirectly, anything that infringes a right under this Part.” Part II then sets out cases in which a right under Part I “is not infringed”, for example by “the implementation of a special program” of the kind section 14 describes. (Human Rights Code, ss. 9, 14 (1), 17 (1), 18)

sections.heading: The protected grounds
paragraphs: For services, the listed grounds are “race, ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin, citizenship, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, age, marital status, family status or disability.” The same list applies to contracts and to vocational associations. (Human Rights Code, ss. 1, 3, 6)
For housing, the list adds “the receipt of public assistance”. For employment, the list adds “record of offences”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 2 (1), 5 (1))

The Code defines some grounds. For example, “age” means “an age that is 18 years or more”. Section 10 has the other definitions, including “disability” and “marital status”. (Human Rights Code, s. 10 (1))

Community Legal Education Ontario describes the same protections in plain words: the Code “says that everyone has the right to be treated equally and not be discriminated against” at work, in housing, in a union or professional group, and by a service provider. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: How do I make a claim to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)

sections.heading: Harassment and reprisal
paragraphs: The Code defines “harassment” as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”. (Human Rights Code, s. 10 (1))

A person who occupies accommodation has a right to freedom from harassment “by the landlord or agent of the landlord or by an occupant of the same building” because of listed grounds. An employee has a right to freedom from harassment “in the workplace by the employer or agent of the employer or by another employee” because of listed grounds. (Human Rights Code, ss. 2 (2), 5 (2))

Section 7 deals with harassment “because of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression” in housing and at work. It also gives a right to be free from a sexual solicitation or advance by “a person in a position to confer, grant or deny a benefit or advancement” where that person “knows or ought reasonably to know that it is unwelcome”, and from a reprisal or threat of reprisal by such a person for rejecting one. (Human Rights Code, s. 7)

Every person has a right “to claim and enforce his or her rights under this Act, to institute and participate in proceedings under this Act and to refuse to infringe a right of another person under this Act, without reprisal or threat of reprisal for so doing.” (Human Rights Code, s. 8)

sections.heading: Disability and the duty to accommodate
paragraphs: A right under the Code is not infringed “for the reason only that the person is incapable of performing or fulfilling the essential duties or requirements attending the exercise of the right because of disability.” (Human Rights Code, s. 17 (1))

But no tribunal or court “shall find a person incapable unless it is satisfied that the needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible for accommodating those needs, considering the cost, outside sources of funding, if any, and health and safety requirements, if any.” In deciding whether there would be undue hardship, a tribunal or court “shall consider any standards prescribed by the regulations.” (Human Rights Code, s. 17 (2), (3))

CLEO explains that for a tenant with a disability, a landlord “must make adjustments so that you can use and access your apartment and your building”, unless this would cause undue hardship. It adds that where a landlord and tenant cannot agree, “the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario might have to decide. In some situations, the Landlord and Tenant Board may also decide.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: I have mobility issues. Does my landlord have to make adjustments to the rental unit for me?, last reviewed March 4, 2021)

sections.heading: Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario
paragraphs: Tribunals Ontario says the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO) “resolves claims of discrimination and harassment under the Human Rights Code”. (Tribunals Ontario, Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario)

A person who believes their Part I rights were infringed may apply to the Tribunal “within one year after the incident to which the application relates” or, “if there was a series of incidents, within one year after the last incident in the series.” The application “shall be in a form approved by the Tribunal.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (1), (3))

A person may apply after the one-year limit “if the Tribunal is satisfied that the delay was incurred in good faith and no substantial prejudice will result to any person affected by the delay.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (2))

A person or organization, other than the Commission, may apply on behalf of another person if that person would have been entitled to apply and “consents to the application.” Two or more people entitled to apply may file jointly, subject to any Tribunal rule that lets the Tribunal direct that an application be considered in a separate proceeding. (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (4), (5))

sections.heading: Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal
paragraphs: CLEO explains that “Mediation is when you, the Respondent, and an HRTO member try to resolve your case before it goes to a hearing.” The HRTO member “will not make any decisions” at mediation. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)

CLEO says that for applications filed after June 1, 2025, “you will have to do mediation first to try and resolve your issue.” For applications filed before June 1, 2025, it says the HRTO will ask the parties to try mediation, but it is not required. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)

If the parties agree, they sign a document “usually called a settlement agreement”, and the HRTO then closes the case. If they cannot agree, there is a hearing on another date with a different HRTO member. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)

At a hearing, both sides present their case to an HRTO member. The member listens to both sides and any witnesses, looks at the evidence, and then decides. CLEO notes: “The HRTO member usually does not give a decision at the hearing. They will send you one later.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at a Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario hearing?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)

The CLEO pages on mediation and hearings were last reviewed on June 12, 2025. Tribunals Ontario's HRTO page says that effective August 17, 2026, the HRTO “is introducing updates to its Rules of Procedure and Practice Directions along with process improvements”. (Tribunals Ontario, Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario)

sections.heading: What the Tribunal can order
paragraphs: If the Tribunal determines that a party infringed another party's Part I right, it may order the party who infringed the right “to pay monetary compensation to the party whose right was infringed for loss arising out of the infringement, including compensation for injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect.” It may also order restitution other than money. (Human Rights Code, s. 45.2 (1), paras. 1, 2)

The Tribunal may also order any party “to do anything that, in the opinion of the Tribunal, the party ought to do to promote compliance with this Act.” Such an order “may direct a person to do anything with respect to future practices” and “may be made even if no order under that paragraph was requested.” (Human Rights Code, s. 45.2 (1), para. 3, (2))

sections.heading: Human rights claims in a court case
paragraphs: If, “in a civil proceeding in a court, the court finds that a party to the proceeding has infringed a right under Part I of another party”, the court may order monetary compensation, restitution, or both. But this “does not permit a person to commence an action based solely on an infringement of a right under Part I.” (Human Rights Code, s. 46.1 (1), (2))

A person may not apply to the Tribunal about a right if a civil proceeding seeking an order under section 46.1 about the same alleged infringement “has not been finally determined or withdrawn”, or if “a court has finally determined the issue of whether the right has been infringed or the matter has been settled.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (11))
